newsitem.title: THAILAND: Death toll in Thai hotel fire tops 80, more feared.
newsitem.headline: Death toll in Thai hotel fire tops 80, more feared.

text.p: More than 80 people are known to have died in Thailand's worst hotel fire and the toll looked certain to rise on Saturday when rescue workers re-enter the badly damaged building after an overnight break.

Police said the search had been further delayed on Saturday morning by concern for the rescuers' safety and the need to take steps to protect hotel property and belongings left behind by fleeing guests.

The death toll from Friday's blaze at the 400-room Royal Jomtien Resort Hotel at Pattaya, about 200 km (125 miles) southeast of Bangkok, had reached 81, including 10 foreigners. Another 70 people were injured, with three listed in critical condition.
Rescue workers said they believed more bodies were still trapped in the ruins of the 16-storey beachfront hotel.
"We are moving in soon and should find more bodies," said Setapan Puthanee, senior official of the Tourist Authority of Thailand.
"The search was called off last night after it was hampered by darkness and lack of electricity," he said.

Setapan said foreigners killed included a Belgian woman, six Hungarians, and three Koreans. Rescue workers said five more foreigners -- one Hungarian, one Belgian and three Koreans -- were still unaccounted for.
The blaze, started by a cooking gas explosion in the hotel's ground-floor cafeteria, spread quickly to upper storeys.
Rescuers said most of the victims died of suffocation after their escape was blocked by locked exit doors.
"It's unbelievable -- the hotel owners locked the emergency exits to prevent guests from sneaking out without paying their bills," a rescue worker at the scene said.

"We all ran for our lives to the fire exit so that we could take the stairway outside but we found the door locked," Sonthichai Yentrakoon of the Electricity Generating Authority of Thailand (EGAT) told reporters on Friday.
Sonthichai, who had been attending an EGAT seminar at the hotel, managed finally to escape unharmed through a door used by hotel laundry workers.
In all, several hundred people -- from EGAT and from two private companies -- were attending seminars at the hotel when the blaze started.
Rescue workers said they had found about 20 bodies, mostly Thais, lying near a locked exit on the second floor. In all about 30 hotel employees died.
Witnesses said a young Korean woman jumped from a mid-level window to her death at the height of the fire. Four police helicopters plucked a handful of people from the hotel rooftop.
Among those saved from the roof were American Rochelle Stein Salmi, 49, and her seven-year-old daughter Rebecca.

Dramatic Thai television pictures showed the pair climbing out of the window of a smoke-filled 15th-floor room, dangling from safety ropes lowered by rescue workers and then being hoisted to the rooftop. Their hometown in the United States was not immediately known.
Police said the hotel's water sprinklers had failed to function because the power was shut off after the fire broke out.
They said most of the fire engines first despatched to the hotel had ladders that reached only to the seventh floor.
Thailand's worst fire disaster was in May 1993 when a blaze swept through a toy factory in Nakhon Pathom, north of Bangkok, killing more than 200 workers.
